newsitem.title: UK: "Euroticism" keeping EMU on track -- economist.
newsitem.headline: "Euroticism" keeping EMU on track -- economist.

text.p: Political will to ensure European economic and monetary union (EMU) goes ahead on time is more likely than not to win the day, a leading economist at one of the world's bigger investors said on Wednesday.
Zurich Kemper Investments chief economist David Hale said the will was so strong that he coined a term for it -- Euroticism.
Chicago-based ZKI manages assets worth some $80 billion, and is part of Zurich Insurance Co.
Hale has just returned from a trip to Germany, and said he was overwhelmed by the level of consensus on EMU among decision-makers.

German Chancellor Helmut Kohl had effectively suppressed debate on the issue within the country by getting most of the major political players on board, and it was clear that he was not going to let the issue of deficit overruns get in the way.
Further fiscal tightening would take place if needed, he said. Latest estimates from Germany's top economic institutes for the German budget deficit in 1997 are 3.2 percent and for 1998 2.9 percent.

But the institute said 3.0 percent was still "thoroughly possible" in 1997. The European Commission said on Wednesday only Italy and Greece were currently missing the 3.0 percent deficit target needed to qualify.
Hale said the EMU focus was now shifting to France from Germany following the calling of snap elections by President Jacques Chirac for May 25 and June 1.
A possible deficit of 3.5 to 3.6 percent in France in 1997 was not acceptable, and assuming Chirac wins the poll, a budget package could be expected in July.
Hale said it was more likely than not that EMU would go ahead, and the first wave would probably see eight or nine entrants with Spain, Portugal and Italy most likely joining in a second wave.

The stakes in EMU were so high that European financial markets were likely to become increasingly volatile as June's Amsterdam summit approached, irrespective of U.S. Federal Reserve actions, Hale said.

"At this point only one thing is certain. The governments of Germany, France, Italy and other countries have invested so much political capital in EMU that the resolution of the issue will be the dominant influence on European financial markets during 1997."
He also said that if EMU went ahead without effective microeconomic reform, there would be recurring crises over its viability during the early years of the next century.
If it was deferred with effective action to revive it later, European financial markets could rally quickly after any negative kneejerk reaction to such a deferral.

"If it is deferred without effective action to pursue the reforms necessary to reduce unemployment and fiscal deficits, the European Union could enter a period of policy paralysis and social strife so severe that it will call into question its ability to cope with the challenges of globalisation as an open economy during the 21st century."
